common_name: Arthur Menzies Mahonia (Extra-Hardy Winter-Flowering Oregon Grape Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Arthur Menzies tolerates both summer heat and winter cold better than most Mahonia x media selections, making it the hardiest choice in this group for colder gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade, siting it where its bold, spiny, holly-textured pinnate leaves and stiff, upright habit have room to develop into a large architectural evergreen. Raised at San Francisco's Strybing Arboretum and prized above other Mahonia x media selections for its outstanding cold tolerance and vigor, it produces dense, upright racemes of fragrant bright yellow flowers in late fall to early winter, an unusually early and generous show that feeds overwintering pollinators, followed by powdery blue-black berries that birds strip through late winter. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and dry shade beneath trees once rooted in, needing only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells. Prune only to remove dead, damaged, or overly leggy canes, cutting them back near ground level to encourage fresh basal growth.
sources: Great Plant Picks — Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Atropurpurea is an older selection of Oregon grape chosen for foliage that turns a deeper, more reliable purple-bronze through winter than the species.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade, giving it enough open sky to color well without the scorching that full sun can cause on hot summer afternoons. Atropurpurea carries the same glossy, spiny-toothed, holly-like leaflets and dense clusters of fragrant yellow spring flowers as typical Oregon grape, but its foliage consistently deepens to a rich plum-purple through the cold months, a trait more pronounced and dependable on this selection than on unnamed seedlings. Dusty blue-black berries follow the flowers and are readily eaten by birds. It suckers gently to form a tidy colony useful for a shaded shrub border or woodland edge, and old or leggy canes can be cut to the ground periodically to keep the planting dense and renew winter color.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Argenteum keeps its crisp white leaf margins best with several hours of direct sun and tends to grow more slowly than the plain green or gold-leaved California privet forms.

directions: This silver-variegated sport of California privet carries gray-green leaves irregularly margined in creamy white, offering a cooler, brighter alternative to the more common gold-margined privet selections while sharing the same tough, adaptable constitution. It works well as a pale accent hedge, screening shrub, or contrast planting against dark evergreens such as boxwood or holly, and its slower growth compared with the species makes it somewhat easier to keep in bounds with less frequent shearing. Variegation is brightest in full sun and fades toward plain gray-green in heavier shade, so give it as much direct light as the site allows. Like other California privet forms it tolerates poor soil, urban pollution, and hard pruning, and shearing before the small white flower clusters open in early summer helps limit self-seeding near natural areas.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Curly-Leaf Ligustrum grows much more slowly and densely than typical wax-leaf privet, so it needs little shearing to stay tidy.

directions: Curly-Leaf Ligustrum is a distinctive, slow-growing selection of Japanese privet grown chiefly for its thick, rounded, cupped, dark green leaves that curl inward along the margins, giving the plant a dense, sculptural, almost boxwood-like texture very different from the flat, glossy foliage of typical wax-leaf privet. Its naturally tight, compact habit makes it useful as a low clipped hedge, foundation planting, or specimen accent in formal and Japanese-style gardens, and it needs only light, infrequent shearing to hold a neat shape. It tolerates a range of soils and adapts well to partial shade beneath high canopy, though full sun produces the densest growth. Established plants are drought-tolerant and largely trouble-free, and old, overgrown specimens can be renewed with hard pruning in early spring.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
